match.reason: Neither bank point teaches the types of coastal landforms (headlands, cliffs, caves, arches, stacks, beaches, spits and dunes): one covers landscape versus landform definitions, and the other covers the general processes of erosion, transportation and deposition, so a new point is needed.

draft.title: Coastal landforms
card: Erosion
Waves crash against a headland, a piece of land that sticks out into the sea. Over time they wear it away and shape new landforms.
Sequence
Waves cut a cave into the headland. If the cave wears right through, it becomes an arch. When the top of the arch falls, a stack is left standing in the sea.
Example
The Twelve Apostles, on Victoria's Great Ocean Road, are stacks. They were once part of the cliffs.
Deposition
Waves also drop sand on the coast. This builds beaches, spits (long strips of sand that stick out from the land) and dunes (hills of sand piled up behind a beach).
draft.remember: Waves wear rock away to make cliffs, caves, arches and stacks, and drop sand to make beaches, spits and dunes.

a.q: A sea cave has worn right through a headland, leaving a bridge of rock over the water. What is this landform called?
a.why: A cave that wears right through the headland leaves an arch. A stack forms only after the top of an arch falls, leaving a column of rock alone in the sea.
a.clue: The rock still joins the land at the top.

b.q: Waves have dropped sand along a bay in Victoria. The sand now forms a long strip that sticks out from the land into the water. Which process and landform are these?
b.why: Waves dropped the sand, so this is deposition, and a long strip of sand sticking out from the land is a spit. Stacks are made by erosion, and they are rock, not sand.
b.clue: Sand is dropped, not worn away, and it is not rock.

wants.brief: Four small side-by-side drawings of one headland over time, labelled in order: headland, cave, arch, stack. Each shows waves hitting the rock at the sea level, with the cave wearing through to an arch and then the top falling to leave a stack.
wants.why: Seeing the stages in order helps students follow how one landform turns into the next.

problems.detail: The card says waves drop sand to build dunes, but dunes are built mainly by wind blowing dry sand inland from the beach. Waves supply the sand to the beach, not the dunes themselves. The remember line repeats this.
The remember line says waves wear rock away to make cliffs, but the card never teaches cliffs as an erosion landform. It only mentions cliffs in passing in the Twelve Apostles example.
Why (a) says a stack forms 'only' after the top of an arch falls. The card does not say 'only', and stacks can also be cut off by erosion without an arch stage, so this overstates the card.

check.summary: Both questions have one clear right answer (arch; deposition forming a spit). The card credits waves with building dunes, which wind does. The remember line adds cliffs the card does not teach. Why (a) wrongly says stacks form 'only' from arches.

Question a, wording: Why (a) says a stack forms 'only' after the top of an arch falls. The card does not say 'only', and stacks can also be cut off by erosion without an arch stage, so this overstates the card.

proposal.title: Coastal landforms
card: Erosion
Waves crash against a headland, a piece of land that sticks out into the sea. They wear the rock away and cut steep cliffs along its edges.
Sequence
Waves cut a cave into a weak spot in the cliff. If the cave wears right through the headland, it becomes an arch. When the top of the arch falls, a stack is left standing in the sea.
Example
The Twelve Apostles, on Victoria's Great Ocean Road, are stacks. They were once part of the cliffs.
Deposition
Waves also drop sand on the coast. This builds beaches and spits (long strips of sand that stick out from the land). Wind can then blow dry sand from the beach into dunes, hills of sand behind it.
proposal.remember: Waves wear headlands into cliffs, caves, arches and stacks. They drop sand to make beaches and spits, and wind can pile it into dunes.
